summary: This proposed standard specifies the Logging interface between a downstream Content Distribution Network (CDN) and an upstream CDN that are interconnected under the CDNI framework. It describes a reference model, the CDNI Logging File format, and the protocol for exchanging those log files. This lets the upstream CDN see what the downstream one delivered on its behalf.

eli5.summary: When one delivery company hands packages to a partner company, it wants a record of what the partner delivered. This sets the format and way for sending those delivery records.

questions: what is a cdni logging file
what is c-groupid in cdni logging
subtitle: How a downstream CDN reports to its upstream CDN what it delivered, using tab-separated log files fetched over HTTPS.

tldr.problem: When an upstream CDN hands deliveries to a downstream CDN, it needs reliable records of what was delivered in order to bill the content provider, report on performance and troubleshoot.
tldr.mechanism: The downstream CDN writes a CDNI Logging File of directives and per-request records, advertises it in an Atom feed, and the upstream CDN pulls it over HTTP with TLS.
tldr.outcome: Both sides share one file format, one HTTP request record type and one pull protocol. Near-real-time exchange, operational events and customization of what is logged are left for further study.

today: RFC 7937 is a Proposed Standard from August 2016, and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The features it leaves for further study, such as near-real-time exchange, are not defined here.

sections.title: The CDNI Logging Interface
sections.content:
The CDN Interconnection (CDNI) framework lets a upstream CDN (uCDN) pass content deliveries to a downstream CDN (dCDN). RFC 7937 defines the Logging interface between them: a reference model, the CDNI Logging File format and the protocol for exchanging those files. It builds on the problem statement (RFC 6707) and the framework (RFC 7336).

A CDNI Logging Field is one atomic piece of information, such as the time a task started or the content URI. A CDNI Logging Record is a collection of fields about one event, and a CDNI Logging File holds records plus extra information for processing them.
sections.eli5: A field is one fact, like the time. A record is a row of facts about one delivery. A file is a stack of rows with a cover note.

sections.title: The Reference Model and Logging Chain
sections.content:
The uCDN uses the dCDN's logs to charge the content provider (CSP), run analytics and monitoring, give the CSP reports and troubleshoot. In the RFC's example the uCDN works with dCDN-1 and dCDN-2, and dCDN-2 works with dCDN-3. A dCDN folds the logs of its own downstream CDNs into what it gives the uCDN, so the uCDN ends up with everything relevant to a CSP.

Inside each CDN the logging chain has stages: generation, collection, filtering, rectification and post-generation aggregation, then the log-consuming applications. Filtering can drop internal alarms and mask fields, for example to hide Surrogate hostnames or protect end-user privacy. Rectification handles sessions that span logging periods; a simple approach is to report the whole record in the period where the session ends.

Only some interactions are in scope. The RFC covers non-real-time exchange of delivery logs from dCDN to uCDN. Closer-to-real-time exchange, operational-event logs, uCDN-to-dCDN logs and customization of what gets logged are outside scope and left for further study. Until a customization mechanism exists, the two CDNs agree offline on the information set.

For HTTP Adaptive Streaming, a surrogate is expected to log each chunk separately, which is why the record can carry a Content Collection IDentifier and a Session IDentifier for later per-session aggregation.
sections.eli5: The big company wants to know what each partner delivered. Partners send in their lists, and each list can include lists from the partner's own partners.

sections.title: The CDNI Logging File and Its Directives
sections.content:
A Logging File is a sequence of US-ASCII lines ending in CRLF. Each line is either a directive (a line starting with a hash sign) or a record. The format is inspired by the W3C Extended Log File Format, but this document governs where they differ. A file starts with a directive group, followed by a group of records, and the first directive MUST be the version.

Directives defined for version cdni/1.0:

  • version: exactly one, the first line, value cdni/1.0.
  • UUID: exactly one, a URN that uniquely identifies the file.
  • claimed-origin: zero or one, added by the dCDN to say who sent the file.
  • established-origin: zero or one, added by the uCDN after it has verified the sender. It MUST NOT be included by the dCDN.
  • remark: any number of comments for humans.
  • record-type: at least one, naming the record type that follows, such as cdni_http_request_v1.
  • fields: at least one per record type, listing the field names and their order.
  • SHA256-hash: zero or one, and SHOULD be present. When present it is the last line.

Unknown directives MUST be ignored, but a uCDN MUST ignore a whole file whose directives break the occurrence rules, such as two SHA256-hash lines. The hash is a SHA-256 over everything before the hash line, written as 64 hex digits. It detects corruption such as truncation, but it does not stop tampering by a third party who can recompute it.
sections.eli5: The file has a cover note at the top (who sent it, what columns follow) and then one row per delivery. A fingerprint at the end shows if the file got damaged.

sections.title: The HTTP Request Logging Record
sections.content:
Fields in a record are separated by a horizontal tab and appear in the order given by the fields directive. Field names use prefixes: c- for the client user agent, s- for the dCDN Surrogate, u- for the uCDN, cs- for traffic from client to Surrogate and sc- for Surrogate to client. Every implementation MUST support the cdni_http_request_v1 record, which covers HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1 and HTTPS delivery and is also expected to fit HTTP/2.

Fields that appear exactly once in every record: date, time (UTC), time-taken (seconds), c-groupid, cs-method, u-uri, protocol, sc-status and sc-total-bytes. Optional fields include s-ip, s-hostname, s-port, cs-uri, sc-entity-bytes, cs(Header), sc(Header), s-ccid, s-sid and s-cached (1 for a hit served wholly from the Surrogate's cache, 0 otherwise). If a listed optional field has no value, a single dash character stands in.

The u-uri is the request URI transformed in a way the two CDNs agree on, for example by removing the part of the hostname that reveals which Surrogate served it. Text must be sanitized: null, bare CR, bare LF and HTAB are percent-encoded so they cannot be mistaken for separators.

The c-groupid is an opaque identifier for an aggregate of clients, such as a country, region or postal code, or a BGP AS number. The mapping SHOULD be chosen so each aggregate holds more than one client. A group of one client is allowed but NOT RECOMMENDED because it can identify individuals; the client element then should change at least once every 24 hours.

Logging headers such as cookies can put long-lived login tokens into a central file. The RFC advises configuring an allowed set of headers and avoiding wildcard selection.
sections.eli5: Each row says when a delivery happened, how long it took, what was asked for, whether it worked and how many bytes went out. The viewer is described by a group, not by name.

sections.title: Exchanging Files: Feed and Pull
sections.content:
After a file is fully collected, the dCDN publishes it and the uCDN fetches it in two steps. The dCDN MUST support the server side of both steps and the uCDN the client side.

First, the CDNI Logging feed is an Atom feed (RFC 4287) structured as an Archived feed (RFC 5005): a subscription document updated as new files appear, plus archive documents that are never modified. Each file is an atom:entry whose atom:content has a src link and type application/cdni with the payload type parameter logging-file. The atom:id contains the file's UUID, which helps a client avoid pulling the same file from redundant feeds twice. A published file MUST NOT be modified.

Second, the uCDN pulls the file from its src URI with HTTP/1.1 (HTTP/2 is optional). Both sides MUST support no content encoding and gzip encoding, which the RFC expects to help with large volumes. Polling frequency, the period each file covers and retention limits are agreed outside the protocol; within the agreed limits the server must keep files available, and beyond them it may answer 404, 403 or 410.

Exchange that starts before a file is complete ("tailing") is mentioned as possible but left for further study.
sections.eli5: The partner posts a notice board listing new files. The big company reads the board now and then and picks up whichever new files it has not yet fetched.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA created subregistries under the Content Delivery Networks Interconnection (CDNI) Parameters registry for directive names, file versions, record types and field names. New entries use the "Specification Required" policy. Adding a directive needs a new file version, and adding a field needs a new record type, for example a cdni_http_request_v2 that includes all of v1 plus the new field.

The RFC also registers the payload type logging-file for the application/cdni media type, used to tell Logging Files from other CDNI messages.
sections.eli5: There are official lists of allowed names. If someone wants a new column or a new kind of note, they register it and bump the version.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support TLS for both the feed and the file pull, and TLS MUST be used with authentication of the remote end, following RFC 7525. The exception is when security is ensured another way, such as an IPsec tunnel or a physically secured internal network between two CDNs owned by one entity. TLS gives mutual authentication, authorization, confidentiality and integrity in transit.

The RFC defines no special denial-of-service protection. It notes that the few valid endpoints can be protected by firewalls or VPNs.

On privacy, the RFC says that the uCDN seeing detailed logs is often not a new exposure, since it already sees much of this at redirection time, but the answer can differ with DNS redirection or different jurisdictions. Log files are also high-value targets for exfiltration, and the privacy tools are the careful use of c-groupid and agreement on which fields to send.
sections.eli5: The lists are sent in a locked pipe so nobody can read or change them on the way. Because they say who watched what, people should be careful about what goes into them.
